body_markdown:
A landmark ruling in France has brought renewed attention to the possible health risks faced by flight attendants, particularly the long term effects of working at high altitude. A French court has recognised cosmic radiation as one of several occupational hazards linked to the breast cancer experienced by a former Air France flight attendant.


The decision is significant because it could influence how occupational health risks are assessed for cabin crew in France and potentially encourage other aviation workers to seek similar recognition.


The case concerns Sophie Lainault, a 59 year old former Air France stewardess who worked in aviation for three decades. Between 1989 and 2019, she accumulated approximately 12,600 hours of flight time, with more than half of those hours spent on overnight services.


The court in Bayonne, in southwestern France, recognised three workplace hazards in relation to her occupational disease claim: exposure to cosmic radiation, passive smoking and prolonged night work.


## What Is Cosmic Radiation?


Cosmic radiation is high energy radiation originating from space. It includes particles produced by the Sun and by other sources beyond our solar system.


People on the ground receive some protection from Earth's atmosphere and magnetic field. However, this natural protection becomes weaker at high altitudes. As commercial aircraft typically fly several kilometres above the Earth's surface, passengers and crew receive greater exposure to cosmic radiation than people at ground level.


The level of exposure can also vary according to flight altitude, route, duration and latitude. Flights travelling close to the North or South Poles can experience higher levels because Earth's magnetic field provides less protection in those regions.


This is particularly relevant to long haul flight attendants and pilots who spend thousands of hours in the air over the course of their careers.


However, it is important to distinguish between recognising radiation as an occupational hazard and proving that radiation directly caused an individual person's cancer.


## French Court Recognises Occupational Risk


Lainault's case is being viewed as an important development because it is reportedly the first time a French court has recognised cosmic radiation as a factor in a breast cancer case involving an air hostess.


According to reporting by the BBC, Lainault sought official recognition of her breast cancer as an occupational disease. She is now in remission.


The ruling could provide a pathway for other aviation workers who believe their health conditions may be connected to long term occupational exposure.


Lainault said her hope was that the decision would encourage other women who had previously been reluctant to make similar claims.


The ruling also has practical consequences for her. Recognition of the condition allows her to take early retirement, while future treatment can be reimbursed through France's healthcare system under the relevant arrangements.


## Why Flight Attendants May Receive More Radiation


Commercial air travel exposes people to cosmic radiation, but the exposure experienced by an occasional passenger is generally much lower than that of someone who works in aviation year after year.


Flight crews can accumulate exposure over thousands of hours. Long distance routes can increase the total amount, while high latitude flights may expose crew members to higher levels of cosmic radiation.


Night flights may also form a significant part of a cabin crew member's working life. In Lainault's case, more than half of her flight hours were reportedly completed at night.


The French court considered several occupational factors rather than attributing the cancer to radiation alone. This distinction is important when discussing the case from a medical or scientific perspective.


## Breast Cancer and Aviation Work


Breast cancer is one of the most common cancers affecting women worldwide, and its causes are complex. Risk can be influenced by age, genetics, reproductive history, hormonal factors, lifestyle and environmental exposures.


Research has also examined whether occupational radiation exposure may contribute to cancer risk among aircrew.


A study reported by Harvard Medical School in August 2026 examined radiation related cancer deaths across more than 500 professions. According to the report, flight attendants and pilots had some of the highest proportions of deaths attributed to radiation related cancers among the occupations analysed.


The study reported that approximately 6.9% of deaths among flight attendants and 6.7% among pilots were from radiation related cancers. These figures were higher than those reported for several other occupations in the analysis.


Such findings can add to concerns about occupational exposure, but they should not be interpreted as proof that cosmic radiation causes breast cancer in a particular individual.


## Scientists Warn Against Simple Cause and Effect Claims


The relationship between cosmic radiation and cancer is difficult to establish at the individual level.


Professor Jim Smith of the University of Portsmouth told the BBC that it is impossible to determine whether radiation caused a specific person's cancer. Radiation protection models generally assume that even small doses may carry some cancer risk, while the level of risk decreases as exposure decreases.


For aircrew, this means there may be an additional occupational risk associated with repeated exposure at altitude. The actual risk for an individual, however, can depend on many factors.


This is why the French court decision should be understood primarily as an occupational and legal ruling rather than as definitive scientific evidence that cosmic radiation caused Lainault's breast cancer.


## Passive Smoking Was Another Major Factor


Cosmic radiation was not the only occupational hazard identified in the case.


Smoking was permitted on Air France flights until 2000. Cabin crew working before the ban could therefore experience repeated exposure to second hand tobacco smoke during their careers.


For employees who spent many years working on aircraft, this could mean prolonged exposure to an environment containing tobacco smoke.


The court also considered prolonged night work, another feature of airline employment that can affect workers' schedules and potentially their long term health.


Taken together, the three factors illustrate the complex working environment experienced by some previous generations of flight attendants.


## What the Ruling Could Mean for Other Cabin Crew


Lawyers involved in the case believe the decision could make it easier for other aviation workers to bring occupational disease claims.


The potential impact extends beyond one former Air France employee. If similar cases are successful, airlines, regulators and occupational health specialists may face increased pressure to examine long term risks affecting cabin crew.


Modern aviation already uses various approaches to monitor and manage occupational exposure. However, the French ruling could encourage further discussion about cumulative radiation exposure, flight scheduling, night work and other workplace conditions.


Air France said that the health and safety of its employees is an absolute priority. The airline also stated that it provides medical support that goes beyond the regulatory minimum. The company said it was not involved in Lainault's legal proceedings and had not reviewed the court's reasoning.


## A Landmark Decision With Wider Implications


The French court's decision highlights an increasingly important issue in aviation: the long term health effects of spending thousands of hours in the sky.


For occasional travellers, cosmic radiation exposure during a flight is generally considered relatively small. For professional aircrew, however, repeated exposure over decades can produce a much greater cumulative dose.


The case involving Sophie Lainault does not establish that cosmic radiation alone caused her breast cancer. Instead, it represents a significant legal recognition of cosmic radiation as one occupational hazard among several that may be relevant to a flight attendant's health.


As more research examines radiation exposure among pilots and cabin crew, the aviation industry may continue to reassess how occupational health risks are managed.


For flight attendants, the ruling could also provide greater awareness that workplace health concerns can extend beyond the immediate risks of turbulence, fatigue and physical demands. Long term exposure to environmental factors may also deserve attention.


Ultimately, the French decision could become an important reference point in future discussions about **flight attendant health risks, cosmic radiation exposure, breast cancer and occupational disease** .


### Sources


- BBC News, published 26 August 2026.
- Harvard Medical School, “Pilots, flight attendants have greater risk of radiation-related cancer death than other professions,” August 2026.
- UK Parliament, Science and Technology Committee material concerning cosmic radiation exposure during air travel.


### Disclaimer


This article is for general informational and educational purposes only. It is not medical or legal advice and should not be used to diagnose, treat or determine the cause of cancer or any other health condition. The French court's decision represents a legal determination in a specific occupational case and does not establish that cosmic radiation directly causes breast cancer in every flight attendant. Anyone concerned about occupational radiation exposure, cancer risk or an employment related health claim should consult an appropriately qualified medical or legal professional.
